extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Milton, literary editors, and readers of seventeenth-century English prose
extracted.subtask_description: Annotated edition and critical notes for John Milton's Areopagitica (prose polemic on licensing and liberty of the press), with editorial commentary on language, usage, and historical context. The page mixes the primary text and scholarly notes for readers and editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty to know, utter, and argue
rubrics_metrics.description: "Give me the liberty to know, to utter, and to argue freely according to conscience, above all liberties."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative principle for evaluating publishing and speech: intellectual liberty is the priority liberty that enables other liberties and learning. The passage argues that preventing free utterance will choke growth of knowledge and reduce a people to ignorance; therefore avoid laws or practices that curtail free arguing and publishing. Anti-patterns: imposing prior restraints that make people "less capable, less knowing, less eagerly pursuing of the truth."

rubrics_metrics.name: Against prior licensing; prefer accountability by registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation: "that no book be Printed, unlesse the Printers and the Authors name, or at least the Printers be register'd."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy criterion for producing and regulating printed works: avoid a prior-licensing regime and instead require identification/registration of printers (and authors where feasible). Rationale given: licensing concentrates power, enables monopolists, and suppresses truth; registration allows post-publication accountability. The text also notes historical practice and abuses (Star-chamber decrees, patentees/monopolizers). Practical (historical) enforcement guidance mentioned: for mischievous or libellous works that escape registration, post-publication remedies (historically 'the fire and the executioner') were cited as the 'most effectuall remedy'—this reflects period practice rather than a modern recommendation but is presented as part of the argument about how to handle abuses without prior censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow free and open encounter between Truth and Falsehood
rubrics_metrics.description: "Let her and Falshood grapple; who ever knew Truth put to the worst in a free and open encounter? Her confuting is the best and surest suppressing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation principle for public discourse and publication: the strongest method to expose error is open debate and publication, not suppression. Thus material should generally be judged in the arena of argument rather than by preventive prohibition. Anti-patterns: using licensing or narrow bridges of permission to shield error from challenge; using procedural hurdles to prevent adversaries from presenting arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance of non-fundamental differences (within limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument that "those neighboring differences, or rather indifferences... need not interrupt the unity of Spirit" and that many separations are "more wholesome, more prudent, and more Christian: that many be tolerated rather than all compell'd."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for ecclesiastical and social judgment: tolerate variations in doctrine or discipline that are not fundamental to faith. Exceptions explicitly named: do not tolerate 'Popery and open superstition' (which should be extirpated) nor 'those which is impious or evil absolutely either against faith or manners'—such things no law can permit. Guidance: use charitable and compassionate means to win the weak; distinguish harmless difference from pernicious error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reproducing oppressive controls when defending liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Warning that to repress free opinion one must "first make yourselves... oppressive, arbitrary, and tyrannous"—a criticism of returning to old oppressive practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for legislators/governors and for evaluators of policy: laws and controls intended to curb perceived disorder can, if reenacted, recreate the tyranny they once removed. Evaluate proposed restrictions by whether they would reinstate arbitrary power; if so, reject them. Anti-patterns: camouflaging restrictive, monopolistic, or coercive measures as 'order' or 'prudence.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against monopolies and vested interests in the book trade
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that licensing/Orders were possibly procured by 'old patentees and monopolizers in the trade of book-selling' to exercise superiority and make neighbours vassals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory/design criterion: watch for capture of publishing-regulation mechanisms by commercial interests; ensure publishing rules do not grant exclusivities that favour patentees/monopolists. Scrutinize motives behind proposed registration/licensing—if the effect is to entrench a few sellers, it is harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage disputation, writing, and public argument as signs of a healthy intellectual climate
rubrics_metrics.description: "Where there is much desire to learn, there of necessity will be much arguing, much writing, many opinions; for opinion in good men is but knowledge in the making."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural/educational criterion: treat abundant public disputation and publication as evidence of intellectual vitality rather than diseased schism. Policies or editorial practices should not conflate vigorous argumentation with harmful disorder. Anti-patterns: treating every new opinion as a threat rather than as a stage in development of knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial tolerance for period syntactical variation (anacoluthon etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Note: the Greek grammarians called an 'anacoluthon' a syntactical 'non sequitur' or incoherence; 'Such carelessnesses are common in Milton's prose writings... till Dryden introduced a more correct style.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline for editors and literary critics: when editing seventeenth-century prose, allow for period usages and nonstandard syntax that were common in the era. Do not impose exclusively modern grammatical norms; instead annotate and compare classical or contemporaneous uses (examples provided). Use notes to explain archaic constructions rather than 'correcting' them silently.
